aiOverview.content: In Kenya, data centres are regulated by the Communications Authority of Kenya (CA) under its updated Unified Licensing Framework (ULF), while power-related installations (such as off-grid or captive power systems above 1 megawatt) fall under the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA).CA Licensing Framework: The Communications Authority formally incorporates commercial data centres into its market structure under Network Facilities Provider (NFP) Tier 1 and Tier  (and colocation under NFP-T2 / Application Service Provider categories).Licence Costs: Fees for data centre and related telecommunications infrastructure licences can scale up to KSh 15 million depending on the tier.Power & EPRA Thresholds: Any data centre or private energy facility generating or consuming power above 1 megawatt (MW) requires direct licensing and compliance oversight from EPRA.Data Localisation: Section 50 of the Data Protection Act (2019) governs the local storage and processing requirements for sensitive national, health, education, and financial data.Tenders and InfrastructureElectrical and Contracting Tenders: Public and state agencies (such as the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority and regional infrastructure boards) regularly publish electrical, MEP, and site-works tenders requiring dual compliance with EPRA registration requirements and National Construction Authority (NCA) accreditation.Key Platforms: Current infrastructure and big-data/electrical project bids can be tracked via portals like KenyaTenders or TendersOnTime.If you are looking for specific information, let me know:Are you searching for a current active tender notice (e.g., electrical, solar, or construction)?Do you need details on EPRA licensing limits for a specific megawatt-scale power setup?If you are looking for specific information, let me know:AI responses may include mistakes. aiOverview.content: Kenya is expanding its digital infrastructure in 2026 with new AI data centers, subsea cables, terrestrial fibre links, and dedicated regulatory frameworks.Dedicated Licensing: Kenya’s Communications Authority has proposed a standalone licensing framework for data centres to shift them out of traditional telecom rules and recognize them as critical national assets.Mombasa AI Hub: Mombasa is set to host a Sh194 billion AI data centre alongside its existing coastal tech infrastructure.EU Partnerships: Kenya is in talks with the European Union to mobilize investment for AI computing facilities, broader fibre networks, and expanded data centers under a 10-year digital plan running to 2032.Investment Zones Proposal: Analysts advocate for coordinated data-centre investment zones mapped directly to renewable power (such as Olkaria geothermal), fibre, and water resources.Submarine Cables & Coastal LandingLuLu Subsea Cable: Kenya unveiled LuLu, the country's first fully protected coastal submarine cable system.Mombasa Hub Status: Mombasa hosts at least eight international submarine internet cables, serving as a primary East African gateway.Fibre Networks & Regional ConnectivityTanzania-Kenya Cross-Border Link: State-owned Tanzania Telecommunications Corporation (TTLC) and Kenya’s ICT Authority (ICTA) launched a terrestrial fibre link connecting Dar-es-Salaam and Mombasa via Lunga Lunga/Horohoro to boost regional routing resilience.Northern Kenya Expansion: A multi-shilling rural and northern digital highway project is actively trenching and laying fiber alongside road expansions.Juba-Nairobi Link: The Eldoret-to-Juba (South Sudan) cross-border fibre project via Nadapal continues phased rollout supported by regional partners.Internet Exchange Points (IXPs)LINX Nairobi & Mombasa: LINX Nairobi (operating across three capital data center locations) continues to anchor East African peering, alongside expansions tied to coastal landing points.Asteroid IXP: Operates neutral interconnection facilities inside carrier-neutral hubs like PAIX in Nairobi to lower international bandwidth costs for financial institutions and ISPs.Would you like more details
